Meshillemoth
meh-SHIL-eh-moth
n. (proper name; an Ephraimite father, and a priestly ancestor in Nehemiah)
Hebrew Meshillemoth, a plural form from shalam, to requite — meaning recompenses or retributions.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · In the Text · Related

Biblical Definition

The name belongs to two men. The first stands behind one of the most remarkable acts of mercy in the Old Testament: “Then certain of the heads of the children of Ephraim, Azariah the son of Johanan, Berechiah the son of Meshillemoth, and Jehizkiah the son of Shallum, and Amasa the son of Hadlai, stood up against them that came from the war” (2 Chronicles 28:12). Israel had taken two hundred thousand captives from Judah; the prophet Oded met the army and told them to send them home; and four named Ephraimites stood in the road and stopped their own victorious troops. What they then did is in the next verses — they clothed the naked captives, shod them, fed them, anointed them, carried the feeble on asses, and brought them to Jericho. The second Meshillemoth is a priestly ancestor at Nehemiah 11:13. The Authorized Version uses the name twice. The dictionary notes the word's meaning: recompenses. Four men whose fathers' names spoke of requital gave their enemies food and clothing, which is the law's own instruction and the apostle's: if thine enemy hunger, feed him.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) gives no entry for Meshillemoth; the name belongs to the father of one of the Ephraimites who freed Judah's captives, and to a priestly ancestor.

Webster (1828) gives no entry for Meshillemoth.

The name appears at 2 Chronicles 28:12 and Nehemiah 11:13.

Hebrew Meshillemoth, from shalam, to requite; the sense is recompenses.

His son Berechiah was one of four heads of Ephraim who freed Judah's captives.

The second bearer is an ancestor of Amashai in the priestly register.

Key Scripture

2Ch 28:12 — "Then certain of the heads of the children of Ephraim, Azariah the son of Johanan, Berechiah the son of Meshillemoth, and Jehizkiah the son of Shallum, and Amasa the son of Hadlai, stood up against them that came from the war,"

Neh 11:13 — "And his brethren, chief of the fathers, two hundred forty and two: and Amashai the son of Azareel, the son of Ahasai, the son of Meshillemoth, the son of Immer,"

Pro 25:21 — "If thine enemy be hungry, give him bread to eat; and if he be thirsty, give him water to drink:"

Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.

expand to see more

The reading to resist treats 2 Chronicles 28 as an anomaly, a flash of humanitarian instinct in an otherwise brutal record. It is nothing of the kind. A prophet spoke, four named men obeyed, and the law they obeyed was already written: Proverbs 25:21, if thine enemy be hungry, give him bread to eat. The Old Testament ethic toward enemies is not what it is commonly assumed to be.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the courage of standing against one's own side. Four heads of Ephraim stood up against an army of their own countrymen returning in triumph, and made them give back the spoil. That is harder than opposing an enemy, and Scripture names the four men who did it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Meshillemoth, recompenses, from shalam; father of Berechiah, one of the four Ephraimites who freed Judah's captives.

expand to see more

Hebrew Meshillemoth, a plural form of shillem, recompense or requital.

The root shalam gives both shalom, peace, and the word for repayment.

2 Chronicles 28:12 and Nehemiah 11:13 are the only occurrences.

Four heads of Ephraim stopped their own army and freed 200,000 captives.

Proverbs 25:21 had already commanded bread for a hungry enemy.
